utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stamp, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, the Prosecution is, Mr. President. It is Witness R who is here and available, and I believe the arrangements for voice distortion are in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's also my information. So we will wait until he is brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. I take it that you can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. R, because we will call you Mrs. R, since protective measures are granted in respect of you, protective measures that mean that your face is not visible, your voice is not audible as it is, but will be distorted, and your name will not be used in this courtroom. Mrs. R, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher, and may I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness is not speaking into the microphone. French booth made a mistake, Mr. President. Ask the witness to say it again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you to repeat it because they had some difficulties in hearing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. I will now switch to the -- it has now been understood and translated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you to put off your microphone when the witness is answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, may I proceed by handing to the witness a document marked P3685?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness R, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am going to ask you to look at that document and say nothing until I ask you two questions about it. Thank you, you may close it now. By telling me "yes" or "no," could you answer whether or not you see or you have seen your name and date of birth on that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness R, because of necessity, you have been granted protective measures. I wish to take you directly to the events that you are here to speak about without going into your background in any detail. In the years 1992 to 1994, were you living in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you go anywhere in particular on the 4th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall where in Dobrinja you went to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The place is called Dobrinja I and the area is called Branulatsa Sarajeva, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you go to a particular site in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was a gathering point. We used to barter food items there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was that your purpose to be there, to barter food items?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I needed to obtain flour to feed my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you describe the area where you were, the immediate area where you were involved in this bartering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, I took a longer route to Dobrinja because I wanted to take a safer route that I believed was safe from shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what did you take to barter for flour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I took apples.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you put these apples at any particular place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, they were packed in one kilogram packages and I had them in my bag, sitting next to me. So people who would bring flour would give me flour and I would give them apples in exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were in this area where the bartering took place, can you say whether or not there were other persons there and about how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There were many people. There were people from my neighbourhood. There were women from my neighbourhood who died. Some were wounded, some were uninjured. And there were people from Dobrinja as well. Some of them got injured, some of them were unharmed. I can't remember all of their names. I don't even know all of their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have it here that you said -- I have it here that you said -- oh, "unharmed," I beg your pardon. I thought it was "unarmed." Since you are here, may I ask you: While you were there, did you see anyone with any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anybody with arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said that some of the persons there were injured. Could you tell us precisely what happened to cause injuries, and just tell us what you observed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, we heard this sound of shells, if I can call it that, and a shell landed at that moment between or amongst ourselves. There were many wounded. I was among them. My neighbours were wounded. There were people who got killed, and there were people from Dobrinja as well whom I don't know, but there were many people. I can name some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's take it step by step and in sequence. Where the incident occurred, what is the first thing you hear, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: We heard this sound of a shell. We didn't know where it was going to land. We didn't even think it was going to land near us because all of us were gathered together, but this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: After you heard the sound of the shell, did you hear where it landed and whether it exploded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: One shell landed further away behind a building. That is how we felt it. And the other one landed in a spot where we were gathered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The shell that landed further away, is this the one that you heard passing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was this the first or the second shell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The first shell. The second one landed in a spot where I was together with my neighbours and other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: After you heard the first shell pass over and explode between buildings, did you and your friends do anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, we tried to get shelter in the building entrance but, later on, we came back because we didn't think that another shell would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how long after you heard the first shell did you return to where you were at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Two, three, perhaps five minutes. I can't really pinpoint exactly. We were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you returned to where you were, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Soon thereafter, a shell landed in a spot where a group of women was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you say the shell landed, could you describe to us what you heard and what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I heard a sound. I couldn't see a shell because there was smoke and dust all over. People were screaming, just like I was, because I could tell right away that I had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I was afraid so I ran to an apartment, and a man there helped me. Other people who could flee, they fled, but some people remained in a spot, and some women remained there wounded until somebody came to pick them up. This is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you taken anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. This man in whose balcony I took shelter, he helped me and he helped me take off my boots. I don't know exactly what I was wearing. So I sat there and a woman came in a white coat, she was probably a nurse, and she bandaged my leg and helped me a little bit. And then they loaded me in a car and took me to the hospital in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were you treated there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I was treated and released that day, and then I had to go daily to renew my bandages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were being taken to the hospital, did you hear anything else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What do you mean, "anything else"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many explosions did you hear that day in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I can't remember. There were many, but I can't remember the exact number. We were so afraid that we didn't manage to count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, was this the first occasion that you were injured in that time period that I mentioned earlier, 1992 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I was wounded in October of 1992 by a sniper, but I didn't give any statement pertaining to that until last year. Nobody asked me about that. And then I gave a statement, and you probably have a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But I am going to ask you to tell the Court about that incident very quickly. Where were you wounded by the sniper? Which place were you at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The place is called Mladeni. I went to get a bucket of water there. There was a well there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you go alone or were you accompanied by anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I was alone and I hurried. I wanted to get water as soon as possible and get back as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Tell us about the circumstances in which you were shot. What were you doing precisely at the time when you were shot?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. At this stage of the discussion, if we want to gain time, the Defence would like to suggest perhaps if we can just put questions in essence on what it is actually in the Defence's brief -- in the Prosecution's brief and not about other facts which are not in this brief so that we don't move away from our point. Because otherwise, any witness could go on about a litany of little facts that we don't really need to concern ourselves with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I believe that part of the Prosecution's brief, and I take it to mean the pre-trial brief, referred not only to -- to scheduled sniping incidents which was indicated that we would attempt to prove in detail, but that they would be referring to unscheduled sniping incidents, and I think that is also reflected in the 65 ter summaries of the evidence -- in respect of evidence of a variety of witnesses. We don't propose to use too much time to go into a variety of incidents, but it is reflected in our brief that we intend to prove briefly some unscheduled sniping and shelling incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The suggestions made by Mr. Piletta-Zanin do not cause me to give you any further guidance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What precisely were you doing at the time you were injured by the sniper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, I felt an impact and I was so afraid that I hurried back home. I wasn't far from my house. I was so afraid, at least, that it didn't seem far. And when I got home, my brother helped me and took me to the state hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were you doing when you felt the impact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I wasn't doing anything. I was simply hurriedly walking to my house because I wanted somebody to help me. I was very much afraid. I was panicked because I was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you listen carefully to the question I am asking you. At the time when you felt the impact, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, I knew I had been wounded. I was about to cross the street, if that is what you mean, to reach the well. So I stepped from the road on to the lawn and I was hit at that moment. I was perhaps two or three metres away from the well and I didn't make it to the well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where were you hit? In other words, in what part of your body were you hit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: In my knee and -- in my knee on the right leg and above the right leg, and I also had an entry and exit wound on my left leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say the direction from which you were shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: From the settlement of Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And on what basis can you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, because that part, that area, can be seen from the spot where I was and we always supposed -- not that we supposed, but this is how it was that they always shot at us from that part of Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the time when you felt the impact, which direction were you facing? Were you facing any particular community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, I was. I was facing Nedzarici. I believe that I would see somebody and would have time to take shelter, but I didn't manage to, and what happened, happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How were you dressed on the day you were shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I had a skirt, a plain skirt as we call it, and a jacket or some sweater. But, generally, the clothes one would wear at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may take you back to the incident of the 4th of February, 1994, you said you sustained injuries that day. Could you tell us what part of your body you got injured at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I was wounded in the left leg below the knee. It was a through-and-through wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you receive a medical record from the Dobrinja hospital in respect to your injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, and I think that you have a copy of that as well. I saw that document two days ago when I visited an office here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That medical record, did you give a copy of it to an investigator of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you sign the copy which you furnished the OTP with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, Your Honours, may I proffer to the witness a document marked P2251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And to the Court that document, as well as the document marked P2251.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could it be given to her off the screen or on the desk in front of her? Her name is on it, and there are protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think the usher was intending to put it on the ELMO, but it should not be. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness R, is that a copy of your medical record from Dobrinja hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see where you signed and do you see your signature there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. I can see it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would it please you, Mr. President, Your Honours, I have nothing further of this witness in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Would you please return the document to the Registry, please. Mrs. R, questions will be put to you now by counsel for the Defence. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us today that on the 4th of February, 1994, you went to Dobrinja. Can you tell us what time that was? When did you set off for Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It was in the morning. It was before 12.00. In any case, it was the morning I was in Dobrinja. I can't tell you the precise hour, but it certainly was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On that 4th of February when you set off for Dobrinja, who did you set off with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There were neighbours of mine who were with me, quite a few of them. I knew some of them. Some of their names I did know, some of their names I don't. There were people with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "neighbours," how many were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Those that I knew, there were four or five, six of us, something like that. It was our gathering point, Dobrinja I, and then we would meet up there. There were about four or five of us, I think, when we went through the trenches, the connecting corridors for the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was a person named Fata Spahic also with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: We met down there. I don't know who came first, whether it was me or Fata, but in any case we were down there together.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if she came before you or you were the one who came and then found her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I can't remember the details, but we saw each other down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which route did you take from the part of the settlement where you lived to get to Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: That was through -- across Mojmilo hill and then through a connecting corridor trench which was dug for the civilians. We went across the Lukavica road and then we went on to Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How often do you take this route?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I only went once on that day. I didn't go before, while the others did go on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you say that that was the first time you went to Dobrinja on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Asked by my learned colleague why you were going to Dobrinja, you said that, "This was a gathering point, this is where we bartered food."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: This is where my neighbours went and this is -- I joined them on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the way to Dobrinja, did you meet a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you warned by anyone that you should not be going to Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, no, we were not told anything by anyone. We needed to go. We needed to get food for our children.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the part of town where you lived, near that part where you lived, did Fata Spahic also live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see troops in that part of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see or did you know that on the Mojmilo hill there was BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that these were civilian trenches, could you tell us where do you have this information from? How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, I think they were for civilians, because civilians used them. Those neighbours of mine who went before, that is what they used. They never said before that they saw any soldiers, any troops. So on that day either, I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How often did your neighbours take that route to get to Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know how frequently they went. I know they did go, but I don't know how many days they went. I wouldn't give you anything with precision because I don't know. But they did go.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After the 4th of February, you were wounded, as you say, on Dobrinja I. Did you see your neighbour Fata Spahic after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't see her for a very long time because I was sick and Fata was also sick because we had to get over our injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point speak about that day, about the day in question, the 4th of February 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We didn't see each other frequently. It would be in passing. We didn't really speak about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before the 4th of February 1994, you spoke of an incident that took place in October 1992 when you were injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were wounded by a sniper that, according to you, fired from Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, at what time did you go and get water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It was 10.00, 11.00, I can't remember. I can't be absolutely precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That source, was it located beneath Mojmilo hill or near Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, no, it is much further, further down from Mojmilo hill. It Is in a meadow near a settlement. It is a well. It is not a source, it is a well that's been dug, dug up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How far is that settlement from Nedzarici where you went for water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I really can't tell you what the distance is. It is not very far and it is not very close, so I really can't tell you. I really wouldn't know. I know that that's where the firing came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How often did you go to fetch water at that source?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, not very often. Later on, of course, when I was wounded, I didn't go at all because I was always afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were injured and you went to the state hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How many days did you stay in hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I did not stay in hospital. They bandaged my wounds, they took me back home. A man came and changed my bandages.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That day when you went to the state hospital when you say that you were wounded, did you get a certificate or a medical certificate from a doctor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is enclosed here. If it is not, then that can be asked for, that can be requested.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you personally have it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't have it with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have the original of the medical documents of the Dobrinja hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I think there is a copy here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you whether you personally, whether you personally have it, whether you, when you went to Dobrinja hospital and then you went to bandages, do you have a document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I have it but I didn't bring it with me. I don't have it on me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But you say you have it at home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On that day when you were in Dobrinja, could you tell us what the weather was like that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, it was a winter day. It was sort of sunny, so-so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When asked by my learned colleague, you spoke about a number of shells that landed. You said that the first landed behind the building and that the second one landed in the immediate vicinity where you were with your neighbours, and after that you said that there were many explosions and that you can't determine how many shells landed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, I heard either firing as I was being taken to the hospital. There was always firing. I never counted it because I was really frightened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information, do you know, since there was a lot of firing, do you know that there was -- there were battles being fought in that part of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you determine perhaps which part of town did you hear firing coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I was in the car. I was being driven in the car. I heard detonations but I don't know from which part of town that was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the part of town where you lived, in that part of town, were there battles being fought?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There were no battles, but there were shells on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "there were shells on a daily basis," could you perhaps tell us whether you were personally present and do you know, do you know about people who were injured or killed as a result of the daily shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, there were, but I don't know their names. I can't remember that. Because, these years, I was mostly at home with my children, and my house itself where I lived was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When was your house shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember the exact year or when it was, but it was shelled. It was shelled twice, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your settlement where you lived, is there a school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, not in the vicinity. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the part of settlement where you lived, did you see armed soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone -- was anyone in your family, close family, a member of the army of BH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you were asked by my learned colleague, you said that you heard a sound of a shell. Could you perhaps describe a little more closely from which direction and at what time did you hear the sound of the shell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I don't think I can say that precisely, not from the -- not the direction or the time. It was in the morning. We were down there. Which exact time, which hour, I can't exactly tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many people were in this location where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you that either. There were a lot of us. I really didn't have time to count people and there was no need for that because we were all scared and we were all just in a hurry to do our business and go home. But, of course --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you spend at that location before you heard the sound of the first shell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Not even half an hour, while we were gathering, and people from the nearby buildings were also coming out. They needed also to barter things with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that you came to that spot to exchange apples for flour, did you know whether on that day there would be distribution of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain how did you know that there would be flour there on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: We were bartering with the inhabitants of Dobrinja. For instance, we would take apples to them or something else, things from the garden, vegetables from the garden. Perhaps they had no flour and they didn't have apples, they didn't have lettuce or something, and then that is how we bartered. That is what we bartered. It was with the inhabitants of Dobrinja that we bartered.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they probably had flour, could you tell us whether you personally knew where they had this flour from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, we didn't know. We assumed because they were near to the airport, they would have it. I don't know why. But in any case, they barter this flour with us. But I don't have the exact information why and how they came to have the flour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they were bartering flour with you, could you tell us that you bartered different vegetables for flour on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, it was only on that one day when I was there on that ill-fated day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That spot where you were standing on that plateau, could you determine in relation to the place where you were standing how far away were you from where the shell landed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There was a play area and a shell fell in a corner of the area where we were standing. There was -- at that time, there was some kind of a wooden bench. At that time, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many persons were killed by the shell that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I know about my neighbours. I know about three of my neighbours, and four of us were injured, and there were others who were killed and injured who were inhabitants of Dobrinja, but I don't know their names or surnames. I just saw them injured and I also heard that there were people who were killed. Because the injured were taken to the hospital just like I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that there were others who were killed, could you tell us who you heard that from and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, it was in the screams, noises, people saying there is people killed, there is people injured, that kind of thing. But these neighbours, I can't give you the names, the injured and the dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us the names of your neighbours that were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Muskija Pribinja, Fatima Sito, Seida - something like that - Balicevac, and I was wounded. You know my name. Fata Spahic was also injured. Then there was Azra Spahic and then there was Refija Balicevac.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are saying that Muskija Pribinja was also killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp. Does the Prosecution want to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I have no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Mrs. R, you have answered the questions that have been put to you by the parties, and the Bench has no further questions for you. That means that this concludes your testimony in this Court. Please be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- be aware that it is important for this Chamber to hear the testimony of those who have been present at these times and at these places, so, therefore, we thank you very much for coming to The Hague. It is a long way, and I hope you have a safe journey home again. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for calling me here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3685, pseudonym sheet, under seal; Exhibit P2251, specialist report in B/C/S, under seal; Exhibit P2251.1, English translation, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These documents are admitted into evidence. May I just make one observation. First, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, when you assisted the Chamber in trying to avoid a waste of time, you talked about the litany of little facts in front of a witness who just testified that she was shot in her left and in her right leg. It would be more appropriate if you would have talked about relevance, rather than of "little facts." I do understand that you meant to say that these were not the main facts perhaps we are concentrating upon. I take it that that was your intention. But in presence of the witness, talking about little facts, if she testified on these issues, that could have been avoided. I am not saying that you could not make the suggestion you made, but other wordings would have been more appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you very much for this remark. What I remember saying - but perhaps I mistaken - is that I said the following: Little facts or more or less little facts. I believe that I may have made a nuance, but I totally agree with you, but I will look at the French text and I will certainly bear in mind what you said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if you would have said "little facts" or "more or less little facts," for a witness, these are certainly great facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are absolutely right, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience. We still have to decide on the admissibility of the sit-reps yesterday when Mr. Ierace examined Mr. Magnusson. We prefer to deal with the matter when Mr. Ierace has returned, so we said we would give a decision by tomorrow, but we would rather do it in the presence of Mr. Ierace. That would be the beginning of next week. Is there anything else apart from that I remember that Mr. Piletta-Zanin is urgent -- is waiting for some information from the Prosecution side on what he calls the "grattage," and I just look at the English transcript, the change of text, rubbing out parts of text, and I think he referred -- was it in respect of the police reports, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, or was it in respect of the medical records?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, in relation to but, in fact, there are these medical documents or quasi-medical in relation to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, could you give some information on it or when did you intend to do it, if you can't do it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We had intended to call a witness to explain how the corrections were made. But having regard to a time schedule and the other logistical considerations, it does not seem feasible to call a witness just for that. However, if the court insists, we will do our best efforts to bring a witness here to explain that. But I am wondering if perhaps an explanation from the well of the Court or from counsel's role would suffice if I could inform my friend so that I can confirm the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we fully do understand that you are under a restraint of time. I think the first thing the Defence seeks is to receive what the Prosecution thinks is the explanation of how these documents were handled. We already had some clues in the testimony which might be possible explanations, but I think before deciding whether this Chamber would like to hear in more detail and perhaps by oral testimony about this phenomenon, I think the first thing Mr. Piletta-Zanin would like to know is what position the Prosecution takes so they can consider whether that is an acceptable position to them or not or how they could proceed to verify whether this explanation is to be accepted at a later stage, whether they have to call any witnesses on it. I think that is the first thing the Defence seeks. So may I first leave it to the parties to communicate on the issue and perhaps only afterwards both the parties, and perhaps even the Chamber, might consider whether it is necessary to call any witnesses or that it is not, or that some of the witnesses that will be called anyhow might have knowledge about what happened. So may I first invite the parties to communicate so that at least you give your views on it to the Defence, and what will then happen, we will see then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. We will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much, Mr. President, for this suggestion. Since we are talking about discussions within the parties, the Prosecution, that is Mr. Stamp, could they perhaps tell us now exactly when he knew about the facts that the witness Richard Mole would not be able to come next week as this is scheduled? This is quite important because the Defence would like -- as you have stressed it yourself, Mr. President, we would like to have the possibility that when we have a problem with an important witness, that we are informed immediately, rather than a few minutes, few hours, or a few days, before the hearing. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is -- the Chamber expressed its view that if there is a major change, and that means not swapping from 10.00 to 11.00, but a witness who takes a lot of hours, that if he is postponed for a considerable period of time, that the Chamber wants to be informed. I think it is quite clear that these kind of surprises should be avoided and, therefore, we want to be informed, and at the same time, we express that we are aware of the importance of quick information to the other party. We also expressed that we are also aware that the Prosecution is not the master of the time and might not always have control over the presence of witnesses. So of course if Mr. Stamp would like to tell you or if there is any specific procedural reason to discuss that in court now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then is there any other issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With your leave, the matter raised by my friend could be discussed as well. However, it is a good precursor to another matter which I would like to raise before the Court. We are trying to move the witnesses through to give the relevant testimony to the Court as rapidly as possible. And having regard to our schedule for next week and problems that we are having, we have been able to arrange for two witnesses who are not on the letter of the 7th of May which was sent to the Defence, although there may have been a subsequent letter. There is a subsequent letter of the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have in front of me this moment a letter of the 8th of May. That is the last one I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that letter indicates that we expect and are in a position to call the expert witness, Berko Zecevic, and also another important witness, I think it is Captain, but perhaps it is Major, Jeremy Hermer next week. They are available and I am not quite sure about the situation in respect to Berko Zecevic, but the captain might not be easily available at another time. But we did ask him to come next week to fill in for other witnesses that we are having difficulties in getting for that week. As regards the Witness Berko Zecevic, notwithstanding the directive from the Court that there be a 45-day period between the filing of the report and the testimony of the witness, I would respectfully invite the Court if they could adopt a flexible approach in respect to that witness. Having regard to the fact that notwithstanding that the report was filed on the 11th -- or the statement pursuant to Rule 94 bis was filed on the 11th of April, all the documents contained in that statement were served on the Defence in both English and B/C/S for -- from sometime last year, and I think even before. And there had been a time when that witness was here in preparation for testimony and he had been listed to testify, and the documents were then in the possession of the Defence. I don't know if it would cause my friends any difficulties or embarrassment if at this stage he was called next week, notwithstanding his designation as an expert pursuant to the relevant provision. And, of course, the situation in respect of Captain Hermer, is a civil expert but he is not an expert and we believe that we would be entitled to call him in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first ask you before asking whether Mr. Piletta-Zanin or Ms. Pilipovic has any observation in that respect, the expert witness Berko Zecevic, you expect him to testify on issues that have been dealt with before in this courtroom, if I am -- if my recollection is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And there are -- there would be one or two added dimensions to his testimony in respect of those events that have been covered before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you -- you ask for flexibility. Did you inform the Defence about what dimensions that you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They are included in the documents which were served in the statement which forms the document to be filed pursuant to the Rule, so the Defence would have been informed of what he is able to say, what he can testify about, for some long time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. As far as new dimensions are concerned, I am not certain that we have the same vision of things, but that is another story. The essential problem, Mr. President, is that your Chamber has a motion which was filed by the Defence and that Mr. Stamp doesn't know about because he hasn't spoken about. The Defence has asked your Chamber to consider that Mr. Zecevic should not be called as an expert witness, for various reasons, and the main reason would be this, is that the report, if we can call it that, has not been done by the decision or order of your Chamber or any authority in the Tribunal but it was done on the orders of the tribunal in Sarajevo, a court in Sarajevo. So in order to know -- because of this, it is not possible to accept that this so-called expert witness should come next week. However, it is true that we have had fruitful discussions with Mr. Waespi yesterday or the day before yesterday, and the Defence would be very happy that the second witness who is mentioned and this Captain Hermer, they can come, and we will hear them with pleasure, that is certain. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. President. I do have to confer with General Galic. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise, Mr. President, but in my worry to be brief, I forgot to add something. If this person should come as an expert, you know that there is a possibility that the Defence has, is to bring its own experts in the Chamber. This is just what General Galic has just reminded me. And then in this brief delay, we will not have time to bring our own experts to be here. So if there are material and technical problems, of course, and the Defence is also not a master of time, and as we all know here, tempus fugit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may, with your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first ask one additional question to Mr. Piletta-Zanin before I give the floor to you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we have seen your written submissions to the Chamber indicating that if a report or a statement of an expert is not made on request of the OTP or of the Chamber, that it could not qualify as a statement of an expert under Rule 94 bis. Could you please indicate what makes you believe that the words, the full statement, of any expert witness to be called by a party would require that the statement is made on behalf of one of the parties? That's my first question. So where do you -- how do you -- what is the reasoning behind this interpretation Rule of 94 bis? And the second question is whether there is any case law in this Tribunal you would rely upon for this interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. But because I am not directly in charge of this problem and Madam Pilipovic is, she will do it for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I usually address the one who is standing at this moment, and you are both standing. So, Ms. Pilipovic please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in our submission, we informed the Chamber that the finding that my learned colleagues are relying upon is the one of Mr. Berko Zecevic, however, it is not the one written by Mr. Berko Zecevic - I think that this is what we wrote in our submission - this is a report made at the request of the court in Sarajevo, and it was written by three experts. So, first of all, we have no consent of the other two experts for that report. I don't have their names right in front of me, but these other two experts wrote the report together with Mr. Zecevic, and also in a case before this Tribunal, the case Kunarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, that would be seen as a problem as well, but a different problem from the one I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I didn't quite follow your question since it was addressed to my colleague. But I believe that your question was: Why is it that we believe that the conditions needed for 94 bis were not satisfied when we say that the expert witness report needs to be submitted in accordance with the Rule 94 bis. I believe that that was your question, why does the Defence believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that was my question. My first question was: What is the basis for the interpretation that Rule 94 bis would not apply if the statement or report of an expert witness is made on the request of some other authority, judicial or other authority, so not on the request of the OTP or one of the Chambers of this -- one of the Judges of this Tribunal. That was my specific question, and as far as I understand you, you raised the issue whether you can use the report of an expert witness or a statement of an expert witness if it is signed and drafted not by one expert but by more of them. That is an issue as well. So I take it that you -- you are informing us about other objections than those I just mentioned. I just mentioned the fact that on whose request the report was made. You now added another issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The position of the Defence regarding whose -- who was the authority that ordered this report is supported by Rule 94 bis. That says that the opposing party shall file a notice indicating whether it accepts the expert witness statement, and so on, and who the ordering authority is. So this is on what we base our position. Your Honour, well, I have just stated our position to you and I wanted to confer with my colleague since we -- we did not envisage that we would be discussing about this question today. So perhaps we don't have all of the information available right now. But the discussion between myself and my colleague was that -- centred around the fact that we would meet with the other side and discuss this matter further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, of course, if there would be further discussions. Let me just confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties would discuss the matter, the Chamber would be able to hear the results of it and I would then suggest that it could be, for example, at the 11.00, if that would be enough time. If not, we would like to be informed about it at 11.00. So then perhaps, unless you would like to make any observations at this very time, Mr. Stamp, or that you...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is one observation. I don't think it is necessary here to say too much in respect to the motion filed. The real issue is whether or not an expert may refer to another document, whether he wrote it or someone else has wrote it, and adopt as his own opinion something which is expressed in it. And I think it happens very frequently, that is something that experts do, refer to other writings or other comments by other experts and adopt it for the purpose of assisting the Tribunal. The real issue here, however, is the one raised last. If, as I understand it, the Court did order that the Defence are entitled to have their expert here when our expert testifies, then if my friends cannot have an expert here in time, then we would not be pressing to call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That would end the debate. However, there is another issue which perhaps our team leader may want to address as to the notice that we should give to the Defence for them to get their expert here at the period of notice. I don't know if the seven-day directive that had been issued earlier would be too long now that we are moving into the last couple months of the case and we would have to be squeezing various witnesses here from a variety of countries in the world and on short notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the -- may I say the time table the Chamber gave in respect of expert witnesses is such that we could expect the Defence to prepare for their expert witnesses to be available within a certain time limit. So of course it is always better if the parties already communicated that we intend to call this expert witness, please prepare for the presence of your own expert witness. But this is, I am afraid, a bit too much of a surprise. The mere availability of the expert report, of course, does not indicate to the Defence approximately when they will have to take care that their expert would be available to attend. And of course, the presence of the expert witness from the Defence is of importance for the cross-examination. It is for sure that, although counsel may be very experienced, sometimes they need the assistance of an expert in order to put the right questions in cross-examination to an expert of the other party. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So the position is that if the Defence cannot make that arrangement to get their expert, we would not be pressing to call Berko Zecevic, and that would foreclose the discussion on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that have been the matter you would like to discuss with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is one of the facts, Mr. President. But in fact, the discussion should be considered as closed, considering that in any case, if this person would be admitted as expert, our expert should be here to hear this discussion. So in any case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you say there is no possibility the Defence could arrange the presence of its -- I mean, just if we would allow Mr. Zecevic to be examined as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is practically impossible partly because of my personal schedule, and I apologise for that, but we have only been informed about it yesterday and today, and certainly because in relation to this person in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, having heard both parties, the Chamber invites the Prosecution to reschedule the appearance of Mr. Zecevic, whether it will be as a witness or as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. As it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any other changes in the schedule for next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: None that I am able to advise about at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do think the Defence has agreed as far as Mr. Hermer is concerned. Yes, I see no objections, so I take it that my understanding was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last issue, if I may raise it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are talking about Captain Hermer, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may just formally tender to the Court through the Registrar the statements of the witness Bajram Sopi, redacted as ordered by the Court, and both the statement of Hamdija Cavic with the attachment, in the form as directed by the Court, and both of them are in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement of Bajram Sopi P3663.B. The statement of Hamdija Cavic, P3663A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they are admitted into evidence, and we all know there is still an appeal pending on the admission into evidence of these statements. Then perhaps the last question to you -- unless you have any other, Ms. Pilipovic, you made me curious. When I asked you about case law, you were about to say something about a decision in the Kunarac case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is right, Your Honour. I have been thinking about that because we had a similar problem in the Kunarac case and at that time our friends from the Prosecution wanted to introduce, as an expert statement, a statement that an expert gave in another case. And the Trial Chamber in Kunarac decided that it was unacceptable. And in accordance with the Rules in force then, it was necessary for an expert to give a full new report, either at the request of one of the parties or at the request of the Trial Chamber. And I can verify the exact wording of that decision. It is dated -- it goes back to 1999, and it was a decision of the Trial Chamber regarding the admissibility of the report by Mrs. Klerin given in another case. The Trial Chamber did not accept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: K-l-e-r-i-n?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is Professor Klerin. I think we will be able to retrieve that decision. Thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is anything else to be raised at this very moment? If not, we will adjourn until next Monday. Madam Registrar, that would be in the afternoon, at a quarter past 2.00, Courtroom II.
